summary:
Greenness Trends in the Nile Delta Region

Function: Analyze 25 years (2001-2025) of NASA MODIS NDVI values of 468 cells with 10 km resolution, along with NASA POWER climate and VIIRS night light data. Interactive map presents either 25 year trends, or year-by-year view via a slider.

Methods: Seasonal correction, trends are computed with Theil-Sen and Mann-Kendall significance tests; automatic p-value adjustment and False Discovery Rate control (468 cells); each cell assigned with a confidence level (high/medium/low). Some of the cells manually verified in Google Earth.

Findings: The regional mean NDVI increased from 0.309 to 0.339, but there are variations: 204 green-positive cells and 178 brown-negative cells. Temperature increased at 5 sites (0.29 - 0.43 °C per decade). No increase of night lights, hence no urban sprawl.

Goal and value: To detect signal from noise and indicate uncertainty, which facilitates planning and research. Limitations: 10 km cell size mixes different landscapes; POWER is a model; 25 years is short; trends prove occurrence, not causation.

Software and hardware: Python programming for computation and statistical analysis; JavaScript for Earth Engine script and site deployment; Google Earth Engine/Google Earth; HTML/SVG website deployment to GitHub Pages; GitHub repositories for code. Runs on regular laptops; cloud processing for satellite imagery.
details:
Nile Delta Trend Detective asks whether the Nile Delta is really getting greener, and whether the trend can be trusted. We analysed 25 years (2001–2025) of NASA MODIS vegetation data (NDVI) for 468 grid cells of about 10 km, and compared them with NASA POWER climate data and VIIRS night lights. An interactive map shows the 25-year trend per cell, or lets users step through the years with a time slider.

How it works. We remove seasonality, measure trends with Theil–Sen slopes and test them with Mann–Kendall. We then correct the p-values for autocorrelation and apply Benjamini–Hochberg FDR across all 468 cells to limit false discoveries. Each cell gets a high, medium or low confidence level, and we check a few cells visually in Google Earth.

Findings. Regional mean NDVI rose from 0.309 to 0.339, but the change is not uniform: 204 cells are significantly greening and 178 browning. Temperature rises at all five points (+0.29 to +0.43 °C per decade). Night lights do not rise, so they do not support a simple urban-sprawl story.

Benefits and goals. The project separates real change from noise and shows uncertainty openly, helping planners and researchers decide where to look closer. We also state its limits: 10 km cells mix land types, POWER is a model, 25 years is short, and trends show that something changed, not why.

Tools. Python (data processing and statistics), JavaScript (Google Earth Engine script and website), Google Earth Engine, Google Earth, and a static HTML/SVG site on GitHub Pages with code on GitHub. Hardware: ordinary laptops, with heavy satellite processing done in the cloud.
